sentences: The hall, the dining-room, and all its furniture, were examined and praised; and his commendation of everything would have touched Mrs. Bennet's heart, but for the mortifying supposition of his viewing it all as his own future property.
Almost as soon as I entered the house I singled you out as the companion of my future life.
Mr. Collins's present circumstances made it a most eligible match for their daughter, to whom they could give little fortune; and his prospects of future wealth were exceedingly fair.
He meant to resign his commission immediately; and as to his future situation, he could conjecture very little about it.

senses.learner: still to come or still to exist; not here yet.
examples: his prospects of future wealth were exceedingly fair.
I singled you out as the companion of my future life.

senses.gloss: effective in or looking toward the future
senses.learner: taking effect later on, or looking ahead to the time that is still to come
examples: The team spent the whole morning on future planning.

senses.gloss: a verb tense or other formation referring to events or states that have not yet happened
senses.learner: used of a verb tense or other form that talks about things that have not happened yet.
examples: In 'she will sing', the verb is in the future tense.

senses.gloss: (of elected officers) elected but not yet serving
senses.learner: of a person chosen in an election: chosen but not yet in office.
examples: The future mayor, elected last week, will take office in January.

sentences: I have a warm unguarded temper, and I may perhaps have sometimes spoken my opinion of him, and to him, too freely.
Miss Bennet eagerly disclaimed all extraordinary merit, and threw back the praise on her sister's warm affection.
They were all of them warm in their admiration; and at that moment she felt that to be mistress of Pemberley might be something!
Darcy, as well as Elizabeth, really loved them; and they were both ever sensible of the warmest gratitude towards the persons who, by bringing her into Derbyshire, had been the means of uniting them.

senses.learner: quickly stirred up or excited
examples: I have a warm unguarded temper, and I may perhaps have sometimes spoken my opinion of him, and to him, too freely.

connotation.why: a milder neighbour of hot-tempered and excitable for the same quickness to flare up

senses.learner: friendly, and ready to respond to other people with feeling
examples: She gave us a warm greeting at the door.
He has a warm personality and makes friends easily.

senses.gloss: having or producing a comfortable and agreeable degree of heat or imparting or maintaining heat
senses.learner: having or making a pleasant, comfortable heat, or giving or keeping in heat
examples: Come inside; the kitchen is warm.
She wore a warm coat in the snow.

senses.gloss: characterized by liveliness or excitement or disagreement
senses.learner: full of life, excitement, or disagreement
examples: There was a warm debate about the new plan.

senses.gloss: inducing the impression of warmth; used especially of reds and oranges and yellows when referring to color
senses.learner: giving a feeling of heat, said most of all of reds, oranges and yellows when talking about colour
examples: She painted the kitchen in warm yellows and oranges.

senses.gloss: of a seeker; near to the object sought
senses.learner: of someone who is searching: close to the thing they are looking for
examples: You're getting warm; the key is somewhere in this room.

senses.learner: made or left only a short time ago
examples: The dogs followed the warm trail into the woods.

senses.gloss: uncomfortable because of possible danger or trouble

sentences: As to art, if she has never tried idealism, her realism is real to a degree which makes the false realism of our own day look merely dead-alive.
But in the first place, he was like him; he is there--alive, imperishable, more real than hundreds of prime ministers and archbishops, of "metals, semi-metals, and distinguished philosophers."
The formality, the under-breeding, the meanness, are there; but the portrait is only half alive, and is felt to be even a little unnatural.
Mr. Collins is perfectly natural, and perfectly alive.
cried Mrs. Gardiner, whose curiosity as to the mode of her intelligence was all alive.

She was more alive to the disgrace, which her want of new clothes must reflect on her daughter's nuptials, than to any sense of shame at her eloping and living with Wickham a fortnight before they took place.

senses.learner: aware of something, used with 'to' or 'of'.
examples: She was more alive to the disgrace, which her want of new clothes must reflect on her daughter's nuptials

senses.learner: having life; living.
examples: The bird was still alive when we found it.

senses.gloss: (often followed by ‘with’) full of life and spirit
having life or vigor or spirit

senses.learner: working or going on; in use.
examples: The old custom was kept alive in the village for many years.

senses.learner: able to erupt, as a volcano still can.
examples: Scientists say the volcano is still alive and could erupt again.

sentences: He had ruined for a while every hope of happiness for the most affectionate, generous heart in the world; and no one could say how lasting an evil he might have inflicted.
To have his errors made public might ruin him for ever.
You are determined to ruin him in the opinion of all his friends, and make him the contempt of the world."

senses.learner: to destroy something, or to make it fail.
examples: He had ruined for a while every hope of happiness for the most affectionate, generous heart in the world
You are determined to ruin him in the opinion of all his friends

senses.learner: to destroy something completely, or to damage it so badly that it can never be fixed.
examples: The flood ruined the carpets beyond repair.

senses.learner: to make someone lose all their money so that they cannot pay what they owe.
examples: The failed bank ruined thousands of families, who lost all their savings.

senses.learner: to break a building or place down until only ruins are left.
examples: The bombs ruined the old church, leaving only its walls standing.

senses.learner: to fall into a broken and wrecked state
examples: Left empty for a hundred years, the old castle slowly ruined.

senses.learner: to take away someone's virginity.
examples: Her family feared that he had ruined her and would not marry her.

connotation.why: frames loss of virginity as destruction of the person
